1:
Why Abraham moved is not stated, and the guesses divide. Gill reports two — that he could not bear the stench of the burnt cities, and that he was ashamed of the scandal of Lot and his daughters — and rejects both on the ground of distance, preferring providence: he was moved about so that it might appear he was only a sojourner. Henry and Wesley report the same two without rejecting them, Henry adding that doubtless there was some good cause. Clarke thinks he was so affected by the ruined cities, and by not knowing what had become of Lot, that he could no longer bear the sight of the place. Calvin allows the sulphur but adds another possibility, that he was driven out by the malice of his neighbours, as happened elsewhere. Ellicott alone thinks the question misconceived: Abraham had been commanded to traverse the whole land, so no reason need be sought, it being the rule of his life to move about, both for his cattle and because by doing so he was taking possession of the country.

On the lie there is no defence offered anywhere, but the accounting differs. Gill calls it little better than a lie, an equivocation exposing his wife and betraying distrust of providence, and notes that good men not only fall into sin but have their relapses. Henry sets out two aggravations: he had done this before and been reproved for it, and Sarah was now with child of the promised seed, so that he of all men should have guarded her. Calvin says he struck his foot against the same stone, forgetting both the chastisement and the favour, and adds the charge of ingratitude, since a man who remembered how his wife had once been preserved to him would never knowingly have risked her again.

Calvin then enters one qualification and Ellicott another. Calvin refuses the reading that Abraham prostituted his wife to save himself, which he says impious men cavil: having long been anxious to live until the promised seed should come, and now seeing his wife with child, he thought of that and not of her danger. Ellicott notices something the others do not, that the thirteenth verse shows the false representation was not an emergency but a standing arrangement between the two of them, and that Abraham never seems conscious of doing wrong in it.

Ellicott turns that into the chapter’s largest remark. It looks cowardly, he grants, in a man with so many trained servants, and to use deceit at the very time when such abundant revelations were being made to him shows an apparent want of faith; but Scripture neither represents its heroes as perfect nor lifts them disproportionately above the level of their own times, its distinguishing feature being that it insists on a perpetual progress upwards. Abraham had not the example of Christ for a pattern nor the gift of the Spirit for aid, and the earlier rescue in Egypt may well have seemed to him a warrant of protection in future difficulties. The wholesome lesson, he adds, is that it was the politic device itself that twice entangled him in real danger.

Why Abimelech wanted a woman of ninety is asked by two of them. Clarke says her beauty must have been much impaired since Egypt, and supposes she was taken less for herself than to secure an alliance with a rich chief who had lately defeated four confederate kings — adding that a second wife carried no disgrace then. Ellicott gives the same political explanation and also the alternative that with the promise of a son her youth had been renewed. Keil and Delitzsch, meanwhile, run the narrative straight through to the warning and the threat, noting that Abimelech had not come near her because God had hindered him by illness.
3:
Ellicott uses the divine name here to answer a critical argument. Because the chapter says Elohim, it has been urged that this is an Elohistic version of the story told of Pharaoh in the twelfth chapter; he replies that the narrator applies the names by rule, so that it is necessarily Elohim who appears to a heathen king, and that the ground for calling the earlier account Jehovistic collapses, since there Jehovah plagues Pharaoh for Sarah’s sake and here, at the end of this chapter, Jehovah protects her from Abimelech — in both the covenant God saving his people from injury.

He then reads the threat medically. Thou art a dead man is in the Hebrew thou diest, and Ellicott takes Abimelech to have been already suffering the malady named in the last verse, so that the illness both explains why he had not touched Sarah and gives the warning its force. Gill and Calvin keep the restraint supernatural, Gill correcting a Jewish commentator who made the visitant an angel when it was God himself, and Calvin observing that God takes greater care of the pious than carnal sense can understand, since he watches over them while they sleep, and that however despised by the world they are precious to him, since for their sake he reproves even kings. Henry and Wesley both note that God revealed himself by dreams not only to his prophets but to men outside the covenant, usually with some regard to his own people.

Whether Abimelech is comparing his people to Sodom is disputed. Ellicott says he is, citing a scholar for it, and argues that though the malady was confined to his household he saw destruction threatening his whole people, who compared with the cities of the plain were righteous; and he adds that Abimelech’s acquiescence in death as the punishment for adultery is indirect proof of his sincerity. Calvin calls that reading perhaps too refined and offers a simpler one: though thou dost severely punish adultery, shall thy wrath pour itself out on unoffending men, who have rather fallen into error than sinned knowingly? Henry hears in the plea the confidence a man may have toward God when his own heart does not condemn him.

Calvin draws two further points from the threat. Since Abraham is not expressly named in it, he takes a general precept to be given to mankind forbidding any man to touch his neighbour’s wife, nothing in human life being more sacred than marriage. And he weighs the plea precisely: Abimelech does not arrogate a purity altogether spotless, but only denies that he was led by lust to abuse another man’s wife, which is the difference between an act of abandoned wickedness and a mere fault — and God both admits and approves the excuse so understood. Clarke observes more simply that God himself asserts the integrity in the plainest terms, and that men outside Abraham’s family evidently knew the true God, the whole nation being called righteous.

Ellicott presses the awkwardness the others pass over. This king practises polygamy and claims the right to take the female relatives of anyone crossing his territory into his harem, and yet his plea is allowed; the words can therefore mean no more than that he was not consciously violating his own rules of morality. That, he says, illustrates the principle that men are punished not by absolute decree but equitably, according to their knowledge, the punishment here being remedial, for his advancement in right knowing and right doing. He ends on conscience: the moral law is often called the law of nature, but nature does not give it and only acknowledges it when given, the inner light being a faint and inconstant glimmering. Keil and Delitzsch carry the narrative forward to the morning, when Abimelech gathered his servants, told them everything, and the men were sore afraid.
6:
God’s admission that he withheld the king yields two lessons. Calvin takes it as proof that Abimelech told the truth about his integrity, then presses the sting: God allows the excuse and chastises him anyway, so that even those who are pure by human judgment are not free from blame, no error being so excusable as to be without some deteriorating admixture. If those unconscious of any evil do not escape censure, what of us who are bound by our own consciences? Wesley draws the other lesson: it is God who keeps men from the ill they would do, and though sin is not from him, it is from him that there is not more sin, whether by checking the inclination or removing the opportunity — so that to be hindered from a sin is a great mercy, whoever was the instrument.

Calling Abraham a prophet is the question of the passage, and each answers it differently. Clarke argues that the word cannot here mean a foreteller, since Abraham was not one in that sense, and that the root properly means to pray, entreat, make supplication — defended from this place, from the case of Saul, and from the priests of Baal, where prophesying undoubtedly means supplication. The intercessor, he says, became in time the public instructor and then the predictor, because to such men God revealed his will; and he twice cites a discourse of his own.

Ellicott takes the older sense of spokesman, especially of one who mediates between God and man, and sets it in a wide frame. There was a true feeling that God in his own nature is beyond man’s reach, which among the heathen led to peopling their heavens with minor deities; in Israel the prophets became an order whose office was chiefly to be God’s spokesmen, and so forerunners of the one true Mediator. On that ground the patriarchs generally are called Christs and prophets. He adds the practical point, that the king is taught he does not himself hold a near relation to God but needs someone to speak for him, and perhaps that he wants fuller instruction, Abraham becoming a prophet to him in the other sense of teacher.

Calvin takes it as a title of honour, or at least of wider import: a chosen man familiar with God, since no Scripture yet existed and God chose rare men to scatter the seed of piety abroad. He then uses the mediation for a controversy. That one man should pray for another is right, especially men who excel in holiness, and such intercession is not to be neglected provided it does not obscure the grace of Christ; but the Papists reason absurdly in making this a warrant for the patronage of the dead, since the Lord does not send the king of Gerar to Noah or any departed father but into the presence of the living Abraham.

The morning after is where Henry and Calvin admire a heathen. Calvin observes that Abimelech, alarmed at the voice of God, rose not only to obey but to exhort his people, and argues from the lesser to the greater: God appeared to him in a single dream, whereas he cries daily in our ears by the law, the prophets, the apostles and at last by his Son, so that it were absurd for so many testimonies to avail less than one vision. Henry praises the reproof as very strong and yet very mild, since Abimelech does not reproach Abraham nor insult over him, and draws two morals: that even the light of nature teaches that adultery is a great sin, to the shame of many who call themselves Christians and make light of it, and that the sins of kings often prove the plagues of kingdoms. Gill and Clarke note only that the king could not sleep after the dream, and rose at first light.
9:
Whether Abimelech is accusing or confessing is the first question. Gill supplies only the connective, that Abraham was in the palace, caressed by the king for Sarah’s sake. Calvin reports the view that the king is not complaining but declaring his own repentance, and answers that his words are confession mixed with expostulation: he may justly impute part of the blame to Abraham provided he acknowledges his own sin, and he does. That, says Calvin, marks him off from hypocrites, who as soon as a pretext for inculpating others is furnished absolve themselves confidently, and think it a lawful purgation to draw others into their crime; no man may exonerate himself on the ground that another induced him to sin. Keil and Delitzsch read the scene politically: Abimelech did this publicly before his servants, partly to justify himself to his dependents and partly to shame Abraham.

Calvin notices why the sin is called great. It binds not one man but a whole people, as in a common crime, and the king could not have spoken so had he not acknowledged the sacred right of marriage — whereupon Calvin turns on his contemporaries, that Christians, or those who boast the name, are not ashamed to make a jest of extenuating a crime from which even a heathen shrinks with horror. Wesley complains of the same equivocation and dissimulation, which however palliated are very ill things, and adds that those do us the greatest unkindness who tempt us to sin, whatever friendship they pretend.

The king’s manner draws praise. Calvin observes that he allows Abraham a free defence, no common sign of a just and meek disposition, since we know how fiercely men expostulate who think themselves aggrieved; the moderation is the more praiseworthy for being shown to a foreigner, and we should learn to let those we accuse answer freely. Ellicott hears a man conscious that his citizens so respected the rights of a stranger and of marriage that Sarah would have been safe had Abraham said openly she was his wife.

Abraham’s defence satisfies nobody. Clarke calls it the best excuse he could make for conduct far from defensible. Calvin allows he did not conceal the marriage with any fraudulent intention, but says he cannot be much excused, since he ought to have been more courageous in vindicating his wife’s honour whatever danger threatened, and since an unlawful subtlety was itself a sign of distrust; and he calls the suspicion unjust, a judgment on a people not yet known, as though all were homicides. Ellicott agrees the condemnation was unjust, the standard of morality in Egypt and Gerar being higher than Abraham supposed, and traces the difficulty to his own imperfect faith. Henry is harsher, listing the distrust of God, the undue care about life, the intent to deceive, the temptation thrown in another’s way, and concluding that even Abraham cannot be justified by his works.

Two then find something to say for him. Ellicott turns the standing arrangement into evidence the other way: that it was settled between husband and wife when they set out proves they over-rated rather than under-rated the risks before them, and though the expedient was a sorry one and shows his faith was not yet that of a martyr, it also shows both of them felt he might have to save his life by a means almost as bad as death — so that after all it was no commonplace faith, but one as firm at root as it was tried. Wesley draws the warning from the other side: there are many places and persons with more of the fear of God in them than we think, who are not called by our name, do not wear our badges, and do not tie themselves to what we have an opinion of — and whom we therefore conclude to have no fear of God.
12:
Clarke uses the half-truth to define a lie, and the definition is the strictest here: any action done or word spoken, whether true or false in itself, which the speaker wishes the hearer to take in a sense contrary to what he knows to be true — anything done or said with intent to deceive, though both may be absolutely true in themselves. Calvin reaches the same verdict another way: Abraham feigned nothing in words, and professed truly that he was Sarah’s brother, but since he had used the name of sister precisely so that none should suspect the marriage, he afforded them an occasion of error, so that though he did not lie in words his dissimulation was a lie by implication.

The relationship is disputed. Gill makes Sarah the daughter of Haran, Abraham’s brother. Calvin, noting that the Hebrew for sister has a wide range, prefers a cousin in the second degree with a common grandfather. Clarke reports an old tradition that Terah married twice, having Abraham by one wife and Sarah by another, so a half-sister. Ellicott takes the half-sister reading and draws two inferences: that Sarah cannot be the Iscah of the earlier genealogy, since with a granddaughter the distinction between a shared father and a different mother would be meaningless, and that her name, meaning princely, suggests she was no concubine but of noble race.

Then a grammatical crux with theology in it. Ellicott gives the rule — that the plural noun for God takes a singular verb when the true God is meant and a plural verb for false gods — observes that the verb here is plural, lists five exceptions, and offers two explanations: relics of a less strict usage, or copyists’ errors, the second confirmed by a Samaritan text reading the singular here. Clarke reports that the plural has been used to argue the word means princes, meaning those in Chaldea who expelled Abraham for refusing to worship fire, but says the best critics and the Jews alike allow the true God is meant. Gill rejects the Targum’s idol gods and notes that many Christian interpreters find the three Persons.

Calvin will have neither. He takes the plural of the angels who led Abraham through his wanderings, dismisses the Trinitarian inference as too subtle, and lays down that wherever a plural verb is added the word signifies angels or princes. The editorial matter printed with him disputes this in his own margin: his reasoning is not conclusive, there are cases where the plural verb still means the true God, and there is no sufficient reason to depart from the received version. Calvin also rejects, and calls most erroneous, the suggestion that Abraham spoke so to accommodate a hearer not rightly instructed — for to what purpose had he built altars declaring himself devoted to the only true God, if he might afterwards deny in words the God he worshipped?

The presents are read against the earlier parallel in Egypt. Ellicott notes that Pharaoh gave his when he took Sarah and then bade Abraham go his way in displeasure, whereas the Philistine gives them on restoring her, grants him leave to live anywhere in the land, and so acknowledges the wrong. Calvin makes the same comparison and explains it: Pharaoh, more severely censured, was so terrified he could hardly bear the sight of Abraham, while Abimelech was composed by the word that Abraham would pray for him — there being no other remedy for fear than God’s declaration that he will be propitious. Henry observes how unjust Abraham’s jealousies were, since the men he feared would kill him were kind to him once they knew. Wesley makes the boldest suggestion here, that God may have withheld children from the pair so long to punish this compact: if they would not own their marriage, why should he own it?
15:
Clarke opens the sixteenth verse by admitting defeat in advance: there is scarcely any agreement among interpreters, the Hebrew is exceedingly obscure, and every interpreter takes it in his own sense. The disagreement runs on three points — what the covering of the eyes is, who or what is called it, and whether the closing verb reproves Sarah or clears her.

On the first two, Calvin and Clarke take opposite sides and each says the other is wrong. Clarke makes the subject neuter: it, the thousand shekels, is to her for a covering, money to procure a veil concealing her beauty from her kindred and from strangers, so that none should covet another man’s wife. Calvin says many interpreters refer it to the gift and seem to him mistaken; the husband is meant, and Sarah is taught that the man she is joined to is himself the veil under which she ought to be hidden, the veil a woman carries being the symbol of subjection and applying most aptly to the married. His paraphrase is a rebuke: hadst thou no husband thou wouldst be exposed to many dangers, but God has appointed thee a guardian of thy modesty, so why hast thou of thine own accord thrown off this covering? Wesley takes the husband too, but domestically — she must look at no other nor desire to be looked at by any other, yoke-fellows being to each other a covering of the eyes, the marriage covenant a covenant with the eyes.

Ellicott sets out all the options and then reverses the verse. The pronoun may be masculine, meaning Abraham ought to have been her protector and failed, but is more probably neuter and refers to the gift; the covering may be a veil against the desires of others or a concealment of her shame. The verb rendered reproved, however, is equivocal and should rather be rendered righted, and it may belong to the king’s speech rather than to the narrator. His paraphrase therefore runs the other way from Calvin’s: so large a compensation for the wrong done in taking her from her husband will prove to all her friends that she has not been disgraced but treated with honour, and in respect of all that has happened she is thus righted. Gill keeps the sting, noting only that in calling Abraham her brother rather than her husband the king cuts sharply at her equivocation.

On the money the two who count it agree. Gill reckons a thousand shekels at about a hundred and twenty-five pounds while allowing they may have been smaller local pieces; Ellicott gives the same figure, calls it a large sum when silver was scarce and dear, and adds that it was the total value of the present, not an extra gift. Clarke goes off into the weights, deriving our word scale from the verb to weigh, and reporting that the shekel of the sanctuary was twenty gerahs and was increased after the captivity — while confessing that on ancient weights very little satisfactory is known.

Two closing observations are worth more than the arithmetic. Calvin raises a chronological difficulty he cannot settle: if Abraham came to Gerar after Sarah had conceived, how could a barrenness become manifest in so short a time? He suspects the order of the history may be inverted, and leaves both opinions undecided. Keil and Delitzsch distinguish the two words for maidservants, the second being used of the concubines the king kept, and argue that the phrase means the preventing of conception rather than of birth. Clarke ends by turning Abraham’s misjudgment of Gerar into a warning against bigotry: such is the narrowness of the human heart that we can scarcely allow anyone but ourselves to possess the true religion, though he who fills immensity has left a record of himself among every people under heaven.
